messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 65

He is 61, a married man who has spent most of his adult life driving city buses along the same routes, measuring his days by traffic lights, weather, and the familiar faces who climb aboard. He talks about his work with the pride of someone who likes being dependable. People count on him to arrive, to keep steady, to know where he is going. It is this sense of order that makes what happened to him feel, even now, like a rupture in the basic structure of his life.

Years ago, while traveling to visit extended family, he is detained by armed men during a period of political unrest. At first he believes it is a mistake that will be cleared up if he stays calm and answers their questions. Instead, he is held for days in a concrete room with no window, then moved, then held again. He is beaten, deprived of sleep, and tied in painful positions for so long that his shoulders burn and his hands go numb. He is questioned over and over about things he does not know. He remembers the humiliation as vividly as the pain: being stripped, mocked, made to beg for water, hearing other men cry out nearby and realizing no one is coming to stop it. Time loses shape. He begins to live minute by minute, trying not to provoke anyone, trying to guess from footsteps outside the door what might happen next.

When he is finally released, he expects the relief to be immediate and complete. Instead, he returns home feeling as if some essential part of him has remained in that room. His wife notices first that he does not sleep. He lies rigid beside her, eyes open in the dark, then jolts upright at the smallest sound. If he does drift off, he wakes drenched in sweat, sometimes swinging his arms before he fully knows where he is. In the first months back, he startles when a cupboard slams or a car backfires. He cannot bear having his wrists touched unexpectedly. Even at home he sits facing the door.

He goes back to work because work is what he knows, and because driving a bus seems safer than being alone with his thoughts. For a while, the routine helps. He checks mirrors, calls out stops, keeps to the timetable. But the enclosed driver’s compartment begins to feel less like protection and more like confinement. If a passenger stands too close behind him, he feels a flash of panic so sharp it makes his fingers tighten on the wheel. Raised voices on the bus—an argument over a fare, a teenager shouting into a phone—can send him somewhere else entirely. He says there are moments when the hiss of the brakes or the banging of the rear door turns into the metallic clatter he heard before interrogations. In those seconds he is no longer on his route; he is back in the cell, bracing.

He starts changing his life in quiet ways. He avoids news reports about war, prisons, or hostage situations. He no longer travels abroad, even for family events that matter to him. His wife asks him to go to crowded restaurants or concerts the way they used to, but he declines with excuses about being tired. The truth is that crowds make him scan every face for threat. He studies exits wherever he goes. He dislikes being in lines because someone might stand behind him. When traffic forces his bus into a tunnel or underpass, he feels trapped and must fight the urge to abandon the vehicle.

At home, he is less patient than he wants to be. He describes himself as “not the same man.” He snaps over small things, then feels ashamed. His grandchildren want to jump on him and play, but sudden touch makes him recoil before he can stop himself. He hates the look of confusion on their faces. With his wife, he is loving but distant, as if some part of him is always guarded. He does not tell her the worst of what he remembers because he cannot stand to see her imagine it. She says he is with her physically but often far away.

What troubles him nearly as much as the fear is the way it has changed his inner life. He used to think of himself as calm, solid, hard to rattle. Now he mistrusts his own reactions. He feels weak for being affected “after all this time,” then angry at himself for using that word. Certain sensations return without warning: the pressure on his shoulders, the taste of blood in his mouth, the helpless certainty that another person controls whether he will be hurt. On bad days he drives his route with a fixed smile for passengers, then goes home exhausted, sits alone in the garage for an extra twenty minutes, and stares at the steering wheel before he can make himself go inside.

He continues to work, continues to show up, continues to move people safely from one stop to the next. But his world has grown narrower and more effortful. Safety is no longer something he assumes; it is something he constructs moment by moment, through vigilance, distance, and control, never fully trusting that it will hold.
